new_statements.quote: Transcriptions of data are adapted to IPA standards, with the following exceptions. [...] and unexpected stress is marked by an acute accent. (The normal pattern is penultimate stress, or final stress if the final syllable contains a mid-vowel.) [p. 273] ... One unusual change which deserves mention occurs in Mariri, which has *n > d word initially and medially. Examples include: *anak > adeʤ 'child', *naŋi > -den 'swim', *nipən > deen 'tooth', *bunuq > -ɸʊdʊn 'kill', *kunij > kódel 'yellow', *niuR > dor 'coconut', *panua > ɸadú 'village' [p. 289] ... Mariri [mqi] *n > d /_ˈV; *k > g /V_V [p. 292, Aru classification tree]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: statement check: group-level-statement. The stress sentence is a transcription convention for all Aru data, restated second-hand from Nivens' (2017) Proto-Aru database (Daigle fieldnotes), not a description of Mariri; about a dozen Mariri forms are marked as departing from it. If kept, note the rule as stated is quality-conditioned (final stress when the final syllable has a mid vowel), so 'fixed: penultimate syllable' is only the default branch. | checker: Grimes & Edwards 2026 (LangSci 526, CC-BY, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18323007) is held as extracted text; its own bibliography and the appendix row 'Mariri mqi mari1430 -6.15 134.88 Daigle fieldnotes in Nivens 2017' (the text) fix the identity.…
new_statements.relation_note: No tone mentioned for any Aru language; stress treated as penultimate-default with lexical exceptions; Mariri *n > d conditioned by following stressed vowel.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Aru comparative data (including the Mariri forms, from Daigle's fieldnotes in Nivens 2017) the stated normal pattern is stress on the penultimate syllable, or on the final syllable when that syllable contains a mid vowel; any word departing from this carries an acute on the stressed vowel. About a dozen cited Mariri forms carry such an acute, and the authors condition a Mariri sound change (*n > d) on a following stressed vowel, i.e. they treat Mariri stress position as a real, partly lexical property.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically 'unexpected' stress marked per word: Mariri ŋamár, -wúy, ʤáŋel, ʤúgor, adíʧ, orɸéɸ, totóo, ágao, kódel, ɸadú, kartáw (final stress on non-mid final syllables, and penultimate/initial stress where final was expected).
new_statements.identity_note: Appendix row 'Mariri mqi mari1430 -6.15 134.88 Daigle fieldnotes in Nivens 2017'; ch. 6 treats Mariri [mqi] as its own South Aru language (single village), explicitly rejecting Hughes 1987's dialect-of-Batuley treatment on historical-phonology grounds. The stress convention quoted is stated for all Aru data in the chapter (Nivens 2017 database), not for Mariri alone.

sources.citation: Daigle, Benjamin T. 2015. A grammar sketch of Batuley: An Austronesian language of Aru, eastern Indonesia. MA thesis, Universiteit Leiden.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Phonology chapter is for Batuley (batu1258) only: p. 31 'Stress is phonemic in Batuley. Although stress most often falls on the penultimate syllable of a word, it is not entirely predictable.' On Mariri it gives only classification (closest relative of Batuley, 78-82% lexical similarity per Hughes 1987; separate language per Taber 1996: 96), vitality (fn. 15, p. 7: under-20s no longer learn it) and notes a ~50-item Mariri noun list collected in 2014, not recorded (p. 12). No statement on Mariri stress.

sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2.2.3.12 'Batuley' (p. 101): 'Mariri is a divergent dialect of Batuley, on the boundaries of intelligibility. The local people consider it a separate language. The mean percentage of lexical similarity between Mariri on the one hand and Jursiang and Kumul on the other is 80%.' Lexicostatistics and sociolinguistic notes only; no Mariri wordlist printed; the only stress marks in the paper are in a Yamdena dialect comparison.
